tldr: We built PhyDEX, a large-scale benchmark that tests whether Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models understand physical laws like mass and friction through tasks requiring throwing objects beyond an arm's reach. Evaluating representative state-of-the-art models revealed success rates below 3%, highlighting both the fragility of pretrained models and their blindness to physical properties.
hero_caption: Overview of the fully automatic data generation pipeline in PhyDEX. It builds scenes, applies large-scale domain randomization across visual, trajectory, and physical parameters, and executes closed-loop optimization in a simulator—from grasp generation to ballistic and contact-aware trajectory optimization—to synthesize high-quality data.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that control robots from language instructions have made remarkable progress. However, most existing benchmarks only evaluate simple contact between the gripper and the object (such as pick-and-place or peg insertion). This leaves it unclear whether models truly understand real-world physical laws like gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution, or are merely interpolating from their training data.

To address this gap, the authors focused on throwing tasks where an object must reach a destination beyond the robot's kinematic workspace. Successful throwing demands dynamic extrinsic dexterity: inferring an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to calculate the right throwing force and release timing. Using the Isaac Sim simulator, the authors built a fully automatic synthetic pipeline combining grasp generation, motion planning, and trajectory optimization to create PhyDEX, a large-scale benchmark of 9 tasks and 35,000 episodes (143 hours).

Evaluating three representative models—generalist GR00T N1.7, high-frequency DynamicVLA, and force-torque-sensing ForceVLA—yielded shockingly low success rates below 3%. Failure analysis revealed two major bottlenecks: a lack of robustness in pretrained models that causes failures before the throw due to visual and grasp variations, and physical blindness to hidden physical properties. Providing ground-truth physical parameters roughly doubled success rates. Similar failure patterns were confirmed on a humanoid robot and in the real world, pinpointing clear challenges for the next generation of robot learning.
contributions: Introduced PhyDEX, a new benchmark that directly evaluates physical reasoning in VLA models through tasks requiring throwing objects beyond the robot's workspace.

Developed a scalable pipeline that integrates grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop ballistic optimization under randomized physical parameters to automatically generate 35K successful trajectories.
Evaluated representative VLA models and identified two primary bottlenecks behind their sub-3% success rates: limited robustness of pretrained models and physical blindness.
Extended evaluations to a humanoid robot and real-world experiments, demonstrating that the lack of physical understanding is a universal challenge across platforms.

sections.heading: Why throwing? Testing the physical laws that VLAs overlook
sections.summary: Traditional manipulation benchmarks focus entirely on direct contact and fail to properly test environmental interaction and physical understanding. This paper proposes PhyDEX, a benchmark that tasks robots with throwing objects to targets beyond their reach, probing their ability to infer and leverage mass and friction.
sections.details:
Recent VLA models connecting vision and language directly to robot actions have advanced rapidly. However, existing evaluation tasks are dominated by pick-and-place, opening drawers, and peg insertion, where the gripper maintains continuous contact with the object. These benchmarks heavily emphasize geometric trajectory alignment. They fall short of testing whether models truly understand Newtonian physics, including gravity, inertia, friction coefficients, and mass distribution.

To break through this limitation, the authors introduced the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity. When a target lies outside the robot's kinematic workspace, the only way to deliver an object is to throw it. Successful throwing requires inferring the object's mass, center of mass offset, and fingertip friction to precisely compute acceleration and release angle.

Using 100 kitchen environments and 107 assets, the authors created PhyDEX with 9 distinct tasks. These cover uniform objects, irregular objects with offset centers of mass, and dynamic objects with moving contents, aimed at static or moving destinations. Evaluating representative models showed an average success rate below 10% (under 3% in fully randomized environments), revealing just how far current VLAs are from understanding physical laws.

sections.heading: Moving beyond geometric tracing toward true physical understanding
sections.summary: While research on language-conditioned manipulation and high-speed dynamic control is advancing, prior work has mainly evaluated geometric trajectory tracking. Explicitly inferring and accounting for hidden physical properties like mass and friction remains unexplored, and this study directly bridges that gap.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Language-Conditioned Robotic Manipulation
Recent language-conditioned manipulation has been driven by autoregressive models and diffusion models (such as Diffusion Policy). While generalization to language instructions has improved significantly, the physical knowledge captured by these models remains confined to interpolating within the training distribution. Whether they can behave according to physical laws in unseen situations has remained unverified.

### 2.2 Language-Conditioned Dynamic Manipulation
In dynamic manipulation requiring fast, reactive control, researchers have explored asynchronous inference to hide latency and extended systems to 6-DoF control. However, evaluations have focused largely on kinematic tracking accuracy, such as following targets in static, predictable environments. This makes it impossible to disentangle whether a failure comes from joint tracking errors or misjudged physical properties. By formulating tasks around throwing beyond the workspace, this study builds a benchmark where success depends directly on physical inference.

### 2.3 Physical Reasoning
Cognitive science shows that humans infer physical properties not just from appearance, but also from prior material experience and the haptic feedback felt upon lifting. While robotics research has explored explicitly predicting or implicitly encoding physical parameters, efforts have been limited to simple placement or contact-rich tasks. PhyDEX rigorously tests physical reasoning by randomly varying mass, center of mass, and friction across objects that look identical.

sections.heading: A simulation pipeline generating 35K throwing trajectories automatically
sections.summary: PhyDEX contains 35,357 episodes (143.2 hours) of throwing demonstrations. The scalable pipeline automatically synthesizes executable trajectories under randomized physical parameters using asset placement, grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop ballistic optimization.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Task Taxonomy and Dataset Statistics
PhyDEX consists of 9 tasks recorded at 10 Hz. Objects come in three difficulty tiers: Uniform Objects with even mass distribution (31.8%), Irregular Objects with offset centers of mass (39.2%), and Dynamic Objects whose mass shifts during interaction (29.0%). Destinations are split across three settings: single static target (31.76%), multiple static targets (29.77%), and moving targets (38.47%).

### 3.2 Benchmark Pipeline
Data synthesis is automated via a scalable four-step pipeline: scene construction, domain randomization, trajectory generation, and data storage.

- ### 3.2.1 Scene Construction
The platform uses a UR5e arm with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper. Based on 100 large-scale kitchen scenes from RoboCasa, target objects, destination containers, and distractor obstacles are placed automatically.

- ### 3.2.2 Domain Randomization
For visuals, three camera poses are perturbed by $\pm 5^{\circ}$ and $\pm 5$ cm alongside lighting variations. For trajectories, the top 64 geometrically diverse grasps are filtered from millions of candidates produced by GraspGen-X, while object poses and initial joint angles are also randomized. For physics, mass is scaled by $0.5$–$2.0	imes$, center of mass is shifted up to $\pm 15$ mm per axis, and friction coefficients are scaled by $0.8$–$1.2	imes$, all independently of visual appearance.

- ### 3.2.3 Trajectory Generation and Closed-Loop Optimization
First, collision-free valid grasps are chosen, and the GPU-accelerated motion planner cuRobo generates approach and lift trajectories. Once lifted, the throwing planner activates. It solves the post-release ballistic equations and uses SLSQP (Sequential Least Squares Programming) to optimize release joint positions $\mathbf{q}_r$, velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}_r$, throwing duration $T$, and flight time $	au$ to hit destination $\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{dst}}$. To handle tracking delays and fingertip slippage during execution, closed-loop replanning adjusts the aim offset via $ oldsymbol{\delta}_{k+1} =  oldsymbol{\delta}_k - 0.5\,\mathbf{e}_k$ based on horizontal landing error $\mathbf{e}_k$.

- ### 3.2.4 Data Storage
Data is stored in Hugging Face LeRobot format. Each episode includes multi-view images, joint states, action labels, and a 2-second history of wrist force/torque (F/T) readings.

sections.heading: Existing VLAs score under 3%: Physical blindness exposed and confirmed on real hardware
sections.summary: GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA all achieved success rates below 3%. Analysis shows that most failures happen before the throw, that feeding ground-truth physics drastically boosts performance, and that these issues persist on humanoid and real-world robots.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Baselines
We evaluated GR00T N1.7 (a representative generalist VLA), DynamicVLA (representing high-frequency 25 Hz control), and ForceVLA (a multimodal model accepting force/torque inputs). Each model was fine-tuned per task and evaluated across 50 rollouts.

### 4.2 Overall Benchmark Results
As shown in Table 1, overall success rates across all models in the fully randomized environment stayed below 3%, with 0% success on moving destinations. Two primary factors explain this collapse:
1. **Limited Pretrained Robustness**: Models struggled with visual and distractor variations, causing around 80% of runs to fail before the throw during the initial grasp (average grasp success was only 21.24%). DynamicVLA, backed by the lightweight SmolLM2, managed only a 3.57% grasp rate.
2. **Physical Blindness**: Among episodes that successfully reached the throwing stage, only 5.6% landed in the target (translating to ~1.2% overall success). The models lacked mechanisms to infer physical quantities from appearance.

### 4.3 In-Depth Analysis
- **Impact of Diversity Score $\alpha$**: Adjusting domain randomization width via $\alpha \in [0, 1]$ revealed that at $\alpha=0$ (no randomization), ForceVLA jumped from 3.3% to 35.3% success, and GR00T N1.7 rose from 2% to 9.3%. High scores on existing benchmarks largely stem from narrow diversity.
- **Providing Ground-Truth Physics**: Appending true mass, center of mass, and friction to proprioceptive features boosted GR00T N1.7 by 12.5% and ForceVLA by 24.0% in success rate, proving that physical parameter estimation is pivotal.
- **Humanoid Evaluation**: In 2,400 episodes on a Unitree humanoid, GR00T N1.7 achieved 6.0% and ForceVLA 8.7%, showing that this challenge is not tied to a specific arm morphology.
- **Real-World Experiments**: We 3D-printed three cubes identical in appearance but with distinct physics (uniform mass, offset center of mass, and lightweight low-friction), testing them on a UR10e throwing into a basket. Vision-only GR00T N1.7 averaged 10.7% success (falling to 4% on the low-friction cube). In contrast, ForceVLA, which senses weight and inertia through wrist F/T sensors, reached 51.3%.

sections.heading: 89% of failures occur before the throw: The path toward physically grounded VLAs
sections.summary: Breaking down rollout failures highlighted two bottlenecks: fragile reaching and grasping prior to throwing, and an absence of physical reasoning. This work points to critical directions for future robot foundation models, including physical sensor integration and reinforcement learning for exploratory reasoning.
sections.details:
Categorizing failed rollouts into four stages—Ineffective Reaching, Approaching Error, Grasping Error, and Throwing Error—revealed that approximately 89% of failures occurred before the throw. Grasping errors formed the largest share at 38.5%, followed by reaching failures at 28.8% and approach errors at 22.0%. Throwing errors accounted for only 10.6% simply because very few trials ever made it to the release stage.

This shows that before robots can leverage physical intelligence, they first need robust approach and grasping policies capable of withstanding broad visual and geometric domain randomization. Across baselines, the lightweight DynamicVLA dropped out at reaching and approaching in 64.2% of its runs, exposing the limited representational capacity of its backbone VLM.

### Limitations and Future Directions
This work focuses on a single dynamic skill (throwing) and rigid-body mechanics (mass, center of mass, friction). Future work should branch out to skills like pushing, sliding, and pouring, as well as complex phenomena like deformable objects, fluids, and aerodynamic drag. Furthermore, combining in-context adaptation to infer physics from brief interactions with reinforcement learning (RL) to explore physical properties through trial and error will be essential for creating robot AI that truly understands the physical world.

captions.F7: Failure mode breakdown across all models. The left bar chart details error distributions for each model, while the right pie chart shows the overall aggregate. Roughly 89% of failures take place before throwing (during reaching, approaching, and grasping).

takeaways: Current VLA models excel at mimicking geometric trajectories but lack understanding of physical laws like mass and friction, driving success rates below 3% on dynamic throwing tasks.
Feeding ground-truth physical parameters roughly doubles success rates, highlighting the urgent need for architectures that estimate or implicitly encode unobservable physical properties.

Around 89% of failures happen during reaching and grasping prior to the throw, showing that basic manipulation robustness under visual and spatial variation must be solved alongside physical reasoning.
As demonstrated by ForceVLA achieving 51.3% success on real hardware using wrist F/T inputs, multimodal integration that directly senses physical interaction is far more effective than vision alone.
limitations: The benchmark is limited to a single dynamic skill (throwing) and does not cover pushing, sliding, or manipulating deformables and fluids.
Randomized physics are restricted to mass, center of mass, and friction coefficient, omitting aerodynamic drag and material elasticity.
Only three VLA models were evaluated, leaving out comprehensive comparisons with large proprietary models or diverse reinforcement learning baselines.
